content: Where did your breakfast come from? Imagine a magic plate that traces every bite back to its origin. Some food comes from the ground, some from trees, and some from animals!
If you eat an apple, you know it comes from a tree. But what about milk? Or honey? Where do they begin their journey before reaching your plate?

content.title: The Farm Journey
content.description: A visualization showing crops growing in fields and cows grazing in pastures.

content: All the food we eat comes from two main sources: Plants and Animals. Fruits, vegetables, and grains come from plants. Milk, eggs, and meat come from animals.

question: Which of the following food items comes from an animal?

content: Look at your lunchbox today! Take a moment to guess which items came from plants and which came from animals. Try teaching your friends how to identify them.
Did you know? Understanding where food comes from helps farmers know what to grow and how to care for animals to keep us healthy.
Make a list of 5 foods in your kitchen and categorize them into 'Plant Source' or 'Animal Source'.
Have you ever eaten a flower or a root? You probably have without even realizing it!
Think about a carrot. It grows under the ground. Do you think it is a leaf, a stem, or a root?

content.title: Parts of a Plant We Eat
content.description: A diagram showing a complete plant and highlighting roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits that are edible.

content: Plants store their extra food in different parts. We eat the roots of a carrot plant, the stem of a sugarcane, the leaves of spinach, and the flowers of cauliflower!
Many people think a potato is a root because it grows underground, but it is actually an underground stem!

question: Which part of the plant do we eat when we eat spinach?

content: Next time you eat a vegetable, ask your parents to help you figure out which part of the plant it is. You might be surprised!
Plants store food in these parts to survive winter or to grow new plants. When we eat them, we get all that stored energy! This connects all living things together.
Go to the kitchen with an adult and find one root, one stem, and one fruit that you eat.
Encourage students to bring a vegetable to class tomorrow and explain which part of the plant it is.
